name: Nasofrontal / nasolabial angle theory

card.summary: Profile-angle metrics borrowed from rhinoplasty and orthodontics that forums use to score noses and brow-to-nose transitions.
card.note: Published norms are clinical planning guides that vary by sex and population; forum cut-offs are informal.

quick.overview:
The nasofrontal angle is the angle at the nasion between the forehead and the nasal dorsum. The nasolabial angle is the angle between the columella and the upper lip under the nose. Both come from facial plastic surgery and orthodontic profile analysis, and looksmaxxing forums use them as shorthand for how a nose looks from the side.

Forum users discuss the angles in relation to brow ridge, nasal bridge height and tip rotation, and some ask about surgeries meant to alter them. Surgical texts give typical ranges that differ by sex.
quick.mechanism: This is a measurement framework rather than an intervention. The angles are read from a side-profile photo or X-ray, and users compare their values with published ranges. Changes are sought through rhinoplasty, brow-area implants or other procedures discussed elsewhere.
quick.risks: The framework itself carries no direct risk. Concerns noted in the literature are that ideal values vary between individuals, sexes and ethnic groups, and that interventions discussed in connection with the angles, such as surgery, carry their own risks.

lead: The nasofrontal angle and the nasolabial angle are two measurements of the nose in side view. The nasofrontal angle sits at the nasion, the notch between the eyes, between the line along the forehead (nasion to glabella) and the line along the nasal dorsum. The nasolabial angle is formed between the columella, the strip of tissue between the nostrils, and the line from the subnasale to the upper lip [1][10].

In surgical references, the nasofrontal angle is usually given as about 115 to 130 degrees, more acute in men (about 115 to 120) than in women (about 120 to 130), and the nasolabial angle as roughly 90 to 95 degrees in men and 100 to 105 in women [1]. These figures serve as planning guides rather than strict standards.

For appearance, the angles describe how smoothly the forehead flows into the nose and how the nose tip meets the lip. Looksmaxxing users read them as a shorthand for brow ridge projection, nasal bridge height and tip rotation, and compare their own profile photos with the published ranges when deciding whether to look into rhinoplasty, brow-area implants or orthodontic and jaw procedures [2][3][4].

chain: Measure the angles from a side-profile photo or X-ray
Compare with published ranges by sex
Identify whether brow, nasal root or tip rotation drives the angle
Discuss procedures such as rhinoplasty or brow-area implants with a surgeon
angle.text: The angles give people a numerical way to describe their side profile, and some use them to decide which feature (brow, bridge or tip) they would like changed. They are measurements, so any change in the look of the profile comes from the procedures or habits chosen afterward.

paras: The nasion is the front-most point of the frontonasal suture, where the nasal part of the frontal bone meets the nasal bones, and appears on the face as a depression between the eyes above the bridge of the nose. It is a standard landmark in cephalometry, the measurement of the head from radiographs, and sits just below the glabella, the smooth elevation between the brow ridges [10][11].

The nasofrontal angle is measured at the nasion between the line down the forehead to the glabella and the line along the nasal dorsum. A related nasofacial angle compares the nasal dorsum with a line to the pogonion, the front of the chin, and is typically about 30 to 40 degrees [1]. Rhinoplasty texts also describe the nose as ideally occupying one-third of the facial height from nasion to the columella-labial junction, and tip projection ratios such as the Goode method, which targets about 0.55 to 0.60 of nasal length [1].

The nasolabial angle describes tip rotation and how the base of the nose meets the lip. A smaller angle indicates a more rotated, upturned tip and a larger one a more drooping tip. The angle is also used in orthodontics, where studies examine how moving the upper front teeth changes the soft-tissue profile around the upper lip [1][5].

Profile angles belong to two clinical traditions. In rhinoplasty, nasal analysis systems divide the nose into aesthetic subunits and segments and give target angles and proportions for planning. The history of the operation runs from ancient reconstruction techniques in Egyptian and Indian texts to John Orlando Roe's first modern closed rhinoplasty in 1887 with Rethi introducing the open approach in 1934 and Cottle advocating closed techniques in 1947 [1].

In orthodontics, Holly Broadbent introduced the cephalostat in 1931 so that standardised lateral radiographs could be compared, and analyses by Downs and Steiner (1953) set out landmarks and planes such as the nasion-based lines used to describe profiles. Cephalometric analysis is used to diagnose growth abnormalities, plan surgery, predict soft-tissue changes and confirm results, with the limitation that a two-dimensional image of a three-dimensional structure can distort detail and that nasion position changes during growth [9].

Several structures influence how a profile reads. For the nasofrontal angle these include the projection of the brow ridge, the height of the nasal root (radix) and the length and slope of the dorsum. Wikipedia describes the brow ridge as a bony ridge over the eye sockets, typically more prominent in men than in women and variable across populations, with the frontal sinuses lying behind it [11].

The nasolabial angle depends on tip rotation, columella position and the position of the upper lip, which in turn depends on the upper incisors and the underlying jaw. Orthodontic studies of retraction of the upper incisors, extraction of four first premolars and two-jaw surgery report changes in lip and nasal soft-tissue profile after treatment [5][8][13]. Typical values differ by sex and between populations, and a cephalometric comparison of 54 Japanese and 125 European-American adults with normal bites and well-balanced faces measured differences in craniofacial structure between groups [7].

sections.h: Procedures discussed in connection with the angles
paras: Rhinoplasty is the plastic-surgery operation that changes the nose's shape, size or proportions, and it can remove a dorsal hump, alter the nasolabial angle or address function. Surgeons may use open or closed approaches, and revisions are reported in about 5 to 20 percent of cases. Cartilage grafts are a long-established technique in aesthetic rhinoplasty, and surgeons assess psychological as well as physical suitability beforehand [1][14].

For the nasofrontal angle, people in forums also discuss changing the forehead or brow side of the equation. Posters describe supraorbital implants, which add projection at the brow ridge, as a way to deepen the angle, and debate whether supraorbital or infraorbital support matters more. Other threads ask whether counter-clockwise jaw rotation is needed when the nasolabial angle is already within range, or what surgery reduces the angle [3][4][6].

Counterclockwise rotation has a separate clinical use: counterclockwise craniofacial distraction osteogenesis, described in a 2021 review, rotates the facial skeleton around the nasofrontal junction to correct airway obstruction in conditions such as Treacher Collins syndrome. It is a reconstructive procedure and is not studied as a way to change the nose profile angle [12].

Forum threads treat a defined nasofrontal angle as part of a desirable side profile and link it to brow ridge prominence. A looksmax.org thread titled 'Holy Nasofrontal Angle' collects side-profile images. In another, a user describes planning supraorbital implants in the belief that they will improve the angle, and replies debate relative importance of supraorbital and infraorbital recession [2][3]. Another thread's title jokes that the poster would give up a great deal for a good nasofrontal angle, illustrating how central the measurement is to some members [15].

Members describe low brow projection or a flat nasal root as 'feminine' profile features, echoing the surgical texts' note that men's nasofrontal angles are more acute [1][15]. These threads reflect how members describe goals and procedures. They are individual opinions and questions rather than clinical findings.

No studies found on the forum use of these angles as a rating framework. Related research exists in orthodontics and craniofacial surgery: a cephalometric comparison of Japanese and European-American adults with well-balanced faces examined how profile measurements differ by population [7], and cephalometric studies of orthodontic and surgical movements report soft-tissue profile changes around the lip and nose [5][8][13]. A study of two-jaw surgery evaluated surgical movement and postoperative orthodontic treatment in skeletal class III patients [16].

Surgical references note that ideal values vary between individuals, sexes and ethnic groups, so the published figures function as planning aids. Rhinoplasty and brow-area procedures carry the risks of surgery, including swelling that can take a year or more to settle and revision surgery in a minority of cases [1].

lore.intro: Members of looksmax.org use nasofrontal and nasolabial angle values as shorthand when evaluating profiles and planning procedures [3][4].

claims.claim: A good nasofrontal angle is a key part of an attractive side profile.
claims.believers: Thread titles on looksmax.org present the angle as highly desirable, with posts sharing side-profile images and discussing brow ridge and nasal bridge position [2][15].
claims.experts: Rhinoplasty texts list typical nasofrontal angle ranges and note sex differences, but no published study cited here tests whether the angle by itself determines attractiveness [1].

claims.claim: Brow-ridge implants or brow augmentation can improve a poor nasofrontal angle.
claims.believers: A poster plans supraorbital implants specifically to change the angle, and replies discuss whether supraorbital or infraorbital support matters more [3].
claims.experts: Surgical texts define the angle in terms of the forehead and dorsum, which implies both brow and nose shape contribute [1]; no study cited here examines implant outcomes on this measure.

claims.claim: The nasolabial angle should be ideal, and its surgical correction or jaw movement is part of an ascension plan.
claims.believers: Threads ask whether counter-clockwise rotation is needed when the angle is already ideal, and what surgery reduces the nasolabial angle [4][6].
claims.experts: Reference ranges are given as about 90 to 95 degrees in men and 100 to 105 in women [1], and orthodontic studies report soft-tissue changes after incisor retraction and jaw surgery [5][13].

claims.claim: Low nasofrontal inclination reads as a 'feminine' profile.
claims.believers: Posters describe a flat or non-existent brow ridge with a low nasal root as feminine and say a good bridge or brow ridge fixes it [15].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that the brow ridge is typically more prominent in men than in women, and rhinoplasty texts give more acute nasofrontal angles for men [1][11].

claims.claim: One set of ideal angles applies to everyone.
claims.believers: Forum threads quote single target values without distinguishing sex or population. [4]
claims.experts: Surgical references give different ranges for men and women, and a cephalometric comparison found craniofacial differences between Japanese and European-American adults with well-balanced faces. [1][7]
